title: Study notes
html:
How to approach a bone image

Always start with a radiograph in two perpendicular views, including both neighbouring joints for long-bone trauma. CT adds cortex, complex fractures and matrix; MRI adds marrow, oedema, cartilage, ligaments and the earliest signs of infection or osteonecrosis; US sees tendons, effusions and the infant hip.

The elementary lesions – the alphabet of bone

LesionWhat it isWhat you see
OsteoporosisLoss of MINERAL, normal protein matrixTransparency, thin cortex, vertical trabeculae, framed/biconcave/wedge vertebrae, Schmorl nodes
OsteomalaciaUnmineralised osteoidBlurred trabeculae, Looser zones
OsteolysisDestruction of matrixGeographic (slow) → moth-eaten → permeative (fast)
OsteosclerosisMore bone per volumeOpacity: focal (snowball) or diffuse (ivory)
PeriostosisNew periosteal boneSolid (benign) vs lamellated/spiculated/Codman (aggressive)
Size changesCongenital / acquiredAplasia, hypoplasia, hyperplasia / anostosis, hypostosis (thinner), hyperostosis (thicker)
Shape changesCurved bone, oedostosis (expansion by a slow lesion)

Fractures and healing

  • Describe: bone and segment, line (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted), displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening), joint involvement, open/closed, physis (Salter-Harris) in children.
  • Healing timeline: haematoma/fibrin (days) → fibrous and cartilaginous callus (1–3 weeks, invisible) → mineralised woven-bone callus (visible from ~3 weeks) → remodelled definitive bone (months).
  • Delayed union, non-union = pseudarthrosis (rounded sclerotic ends, persistent gap), malunion.
  • Dislocation (luxation) = complete loss of articular contact; subluxation = partial loss with malalignment.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip

Ultrasound first (cartilage visible, no radiation, dynamic): Graf α angle ≥ 60° normal. X-ray after ossification of the femoral head (~4–6 months): Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines, acetabular index, Shenton line.

Exam reflexes

  • Osteoporosis ≠ osteolysis: mineral loss vs matrix destruction.
  • Hyperostosis = thicker bone; oedostosis = expansion by a slow internal lesion.
  • Fibrous and cartilaginous callus are not visible on X-ray.
